questions.q: What does plan_generation_num in sys.dm_exec_query_stats track?
options: A counter that increments each time a specific cached plan gets recompiled
The total number of rows returned by a query
The number of indexes used by a query's plan
The number of days since the database was last backed up
questions.explain: plan_generation_num increases each time a plan is recompiled, as opposed to a brand-new plan receiving a fresh plan_handle.

questions.q: Is recompilation itself automatically a performance problem?
options: No — a fresh plan based on current statistics is sometimes exactly what's needed; excessive, unplanned recompilation is the real problem
Yes, any recompilation should be prevented at all costs
Only stored procedures can recompile; ad hoc queries never do
Recompilation only happens during a SQL Server service restart
questions.explain: OPTION (RECOMPILE) deliberately forces recompilation to fix parameter sniffing — recompilation has a legitimate use; excessive unplanned recompilation is the problem.

questions.q: Why is 'the report got slower' an unprovable claim without a recorded baseline?
options: There's no earlier recorded metric to compare the current performance against
SQL Server automatically deletes all query history after 24 hours
Reports cannot be measured with T-SQL at all
Query Store makes baselines unnecessary in every case
questions.explain: Without a dated, recorded snapshot from before, there's nothing concrete to compare current performance against — just a feeling.

questions.q: What common triggers cause a query's plan_generation_num to rise unexpectedly, per this lesson?
options: Frequent statistics updates, schema changes, or explicit sp_recompile calls
Running SELECT statements without a WHERE clause
Enabling Query Store on the database
Restarting the SQL Server Agent service
questions.explain: These are named as common causes of unplanned recompilation worth investigating when plan_generation_num is unexpectedly high.

questions.q: What discipline does this lesson recommend for building a real performance baseline?
options: Capture the same query metrics on a schedule and store them in a history table over time
Only check performance manually when a user complains
Rely solely on the plan cache, which persists indefinitely
Disable autogrowth so performance never changes
questions.explain: Capturing metrics on a schedule (e.g. weekly) into a history table mirrors the capacity-monitoring pattern from Lesson 35 and makes performance comparisons concrete.
